title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Four weeks had passed since Pierre had been taken prisoner. Though the French had offered to transfer him from the soldiers' shed to the officers' quarters, he had stayed in the shed where he'd first been placed.

In burned and devastated Moscow, Pierre experienced nearly the furthest limits of deprivation a person can endure. But thanks to his physical strength and health—which he'd been unaware of until now—and especially because the hardships came so gradually that it was impossible to say when they began, he bore his situation not only easily but even joyfully. And it was precisely now that he found the peace of mind and inner harmony he had previously strived for in vain. He had long sought it in different ways—in philanthropy, in Freemasonry, in the distractions of city life, in wine, in heroic self-sacrifice, and in his romantic love for Natasha. He had sought it through reason—and all these attempts had failed him. Now, without thinking about it, he had found that peace and inner harmony only through the horror of death, through deprivation, and through what he recognized in Karataev.

Those terrible moments he had lived through at the executions had washed away from his mind, as if forever, the anxious thoughts and feelings that had once seemed so important. It no longer occurred to him to think about Russia, or the war, or politics, or Napoleon. It was obvious to him that none of these were his concern, that he had no business judging them, and therefore couldn't. 'Russia and summer weather don't come tied together,' he thought, repeating Karataev's words, which he found strangely comforting. His intention of killing Napoleon and his calculations about the number of the Beast in Revelation now seemed meaningless and even ridiculous. His anger at his wife, his worry about his name being dishonored—these seemed not just trivial but amusing. What did it matter to him that some woman somewhere was living as she pleased? What did it matter to anyone, especially him, whether they discovered that their prisoner's name was Count Bezukhov?

He now often recalled his conversation with Prince Andrew and completely agreed with him, though he understood Andrew's thoughts somewhat differently. Prince Andrew had said that happiness could only be negative, but he'd said it with a shade of bitterness and irony, as though he were really saying that the desire for positive happiness is planted in us only to torment us and never be satisfied. But Pierre believed this without any mental reservation. The absence of suffering, the satisfaction of one's needs, and the consequent freedom to choose one's occupation—that is, one's way of life—now seemed to Pierre to be unquestionably the highest human happiness. Here and now, for the first time, he fully appreciated the pleasure of eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty, sleeping when tired, warmth when cold, and talking to another person when he wanted to hear a human voice. The satisfaction of one's needs—good food, cleanliness, freedom—now that he was deprived of all this, seemed to Pierre to constitute perfect happiness. And the choice of occupation—now that this was so restricted—seemed such a simple matter that he forgot how an excess of life's comforts destroys the joy of meeting one's needs, and how great freedom in choosing one's path—the kind his wealth, education, and social position had given him—is exactly what makes that choice impossibly difficult and kills the desire and ability to have any occupation at all.

All Pierre's daydreams now centered on the time when he would be free. Yet for the rest of his life, he thought and spoke with deep feeling about that month of captivity—those irretrievable, powerful, joyful sensations, and above all the complete peace of mind and inner freedom he experienced only during those weeks.

When on the first day he rose early, stepped out of the shed at dawn, and saw the domes and crosses of the New Convent of the Virgin still dark against the sky, the hoarfrost on the dusty grass, the Sparrow Hills, and the wooded banks above the winding river fading into the purple distance; when he felt the touch of fresh air and heard the crows flying from Moscow across the field; and when light flared from the east and the sun's rim appeared solemnly from behind a cloud, and the domes and crosses, the frost, the distance, and the river all began to sparkle in the joyful light—Pierre felt a new strength and joy in life such as he had never known. And this feeling not only stayed with him throughout his imprisonment but even grew stronger as his hardships increased.

That alertness and readiness for anything was further strengthened by the high opinion his fellow prisoners formed of him soon after his arrival. His knowledge of languages, the respect the French showed him, his simplicity, his willingness to give away anything asked of him (he received the officers' allowance of three rubles a week), his strength (which he demonstrated by pressing nails into the hut's walls), his gentleness toward his companions, and his ability to sit still and think without doing anything (which struck them as mysterious)—all this gave him an almost heroic status among them. The very qualities that had been a hindrance, even harmful, in his former world—his strength, his indifference to comfort, his absent-mindedness and simplicity—here, among these people, made him nearly a hero. And Pierre felt that their opinion placed responsibilities on him.
